questions.q: Why can't you read a qubit's amplitude directly from a `Qubit`-typed variable in Q#?
options: `Qubit` is an opaque type with no readable classical members — the only way to get classical information out is through measurement
Q# simply hasn't implemented a `.value` property yet, but it's planned
You can read it directly, but only inside a `function`, never inside an `operation`
Amplitudes are readable, but only after the qubit is released
questions.explain: The Qubit type deliberately exposes no way to peek at its state as classical data; measurement operations like M or Measure are the only sanctioned way to extract classical information, and even then you only get a single Result, not the full amplitude vector.

questions.q: What is the current, non-deprecated way to allocate a single qubit in Q#?
questions.explain: `use q = Qubit();` is the modern allocation syntax, scoped to the enclosing block. The `using (...)  { ... }` block form is the older, deprecated predecessor.

questions.q: What state does a freshly allocated qubit start in?
options: A random superposition, determined by the simulator's seed
It is undefined until the first gate is applied
questions.explain: The Q# runtime guarantees every newly allocated qubit starts in the |0> state, whether allocated singly with `use q = Qubit();` or as part of an array with `use qs = Qubit[n];`.

questions.q: In Qiskit, what does a qubit fundamentally correspond to?
options: A dynamically-scoped runtime value you allocate and release as the program executes
An index into a QuantumRegister inside a QuantumCircuit object, existing only for the circuit's lifetime
An opaque handle returned by a `use` statement
questions.explain: Qiskit qubits are positions in a static QuantumCircuit object built up front, not first-class dynamically-allocated runtime values the way Q#'s Qubit type is.

questions.q: Why does releasing a qubit that is still in an unresolved superposition typically raise a runtime error on exact-state simulators?
options: Because Q# arrays can only hold measured qubits
Because the simulator can detect that the qubit's state was never resolved to a known classical value (via measurement or explicit undoing gates) before the implicit release at scope exit
Because `use` statements don't support superposition at all
Because only `Qubit[n]` arrays, not single qubits, require resolution before release
questions.explain: Automatic release at the end of a `use` block carries an implicit obligation: the qubit should be back in a known classical state or have been measured. Simulators that track exact state can catch the case where that obligation was never met.
